head: 168a4a1
target: One judge over the run log separates engine invariants from model behaviors and reports cost, so every caller gets the same verdict from the same files.
incidental: the transcript message parser and its shape checks
the token counts and the cached ratio arithmetic
the behavior id format and the per-step cost fields
the inner steps of the nine behavior judges
the test file's helpers that edit a saved run

questions.prompt: The live test used to assert a few engine properties by hand and log the rest. Why does the new judge split every verdict into invariants, behaviors, and cost?

options.label: The three kinds live in three files, so the judge sorts each verdict by its source.
An engine bug and a model mistake need different fixes, so a report must not mix them.
Invariants are cheap to check, behaviors need a model, so they run at different times.
The future grader requires a report with exactly those three sections, so the judge writes them.

key_points: An engine failure is a bug to fix; a model failure is a bet that lost, measured as a rate.
The old test mixed engine checks and model metrics, so a reader could not tell which side failed.
Cost is reported and never judged, so a cheap failure and an expensive pass grade the same.

questions.prompt: A behavior skips when its precondition never happened, and skips are left out of the behavior's rate. Why leave them out instead of counting them as failures?

options.label: A skip means the model chose not to act, and a choice is not a mistake.
Skips are retried on the next run, which adds them back into the rate.
A rate must count only the trials that had the chance to show the behavior.
Skipped behaviors produce no evidence, so a failure verdict could not name their mistake.

key_points: A rate must count only trials that had the chance to show the behavior.
A run that never met the precondition is not evidence about the bet; counting it would punish the run's shape, not the model.
The precondition's failure is judged elsewhere, such as the check that expects the model to enable the plugin.

questions.prompt: The judge reads nothing but the run log that the runner already writes. What does that boundary give its three callers?

options.label: The judge runs faster, because reading the files is cheaper than re-running the scenario.
All callers get the same verdict from the same files, so grading cannot drift from the run.
It lets the judge run inside the engine, where the records are still live.
The callers keep their own assertions, and the judge only adds the ones they share.

key_points: The live test, the command line, and the future grader all get the same verdict from the same files.
A verdict graded later from the files cannot drift from what the run did.
Each verdict carries evidence that names the mistake, so a reader needs no other record.

questions.prompt: Suppose the judge read only the event stream and never the transcript. Which of these would break?

options.label: The judge could not see which plugins the model enabled during a prompt.
A call to a plugin enabled at session start would look like a violation.
A gate's denial would leave no trace for the judge to find.
A tool call rejected before it ran would leave no trace to recover from.

key_points: No listener sees the records a session writes at its creation, so the enabled-at-start set comes from the transcript.
A call rejected before it runs leaves no tool event, only an error result in the transcript under the same id.
The events still carry the records the model's own enables write, and denials at tool end.

questions.prompt: A new rule arrives: every tool call a prompt starts must end with a result before the prompt ends. Where does this rule go, and what must you add so the build passes?
key_points: It is an invariant: the engine owns it, every run must keep it, and it never skips.
It goes in the invariants table, which the report's keys and the typed test table both follow; it needs no declaration in a scenario.
The build fails until the test table holds a passing case and a failing case for it.
Its failing case is a correct run with one injected fault, because no model script can break a correct engine.

questions.prompt: A run has four prompts. The second ends in a provider error, so the run stops there. What does the report say?

options.label: A behavior on the fourth prompt fails, because the model never answered it.
The invariants are still judged, on what the run did before it stopped.
The run counts as complete, because the error came from the provider and not the engine.
A behavior on the fourth prompt skips, and its rate leaves the run out.

key_points: Invariants never skip; they are judged on whatever the run did, even a partial run.
A behavior on a step that never ran skips, and its rate leaves the run out.
The report marks the run incomplete when a scenario step did not run.
